meta.title: GPUs, TPUs, and AI Hardware
meta.thesis: GPUs, TPUs, and AI Hardware is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: An infra team chooses hardware for batch embeddings, fine-tuning, and online inference. By the end, they should be able to build or review hardware selection worksheet for GPU, TPU, memory, and utilization needs, measure utilization and throughput per dollar, and catch the failure where the selected accelerator is fast but memory-bound for the real workload.

modules.title: Start with the workload, not the chip
modules.sub: Classify training, batch inference, and interactive serving before comparing hardware.
modules.summary: Beginner hardware literacy means asking what work must finish, how fast, with how much memory, and at what cost.
objectives: Separate training, batch inference, and interactive serving.
Explain why memory can matter more than raw speed.
Describe cost per useful result in plain language.

spans.text: Problem anchor: a small team wants to run three AI jobs: nightly embedding of new documents, live chat over a 7B model, and occasional fine-tuning. The beginner mistake is to ask, "Which GPU should we buy?" The better question is, "What job, latency, batch size, memory, and utilization are we buying for?"

A CPU can be enough for small classical models, light batch jobs, and orchestration. A GPU helps when large tensor operations dominate and the model fits memory. A TPU can be compelling in ecosystems designed for it, especially large training or batch workloads, but it changes the software and platform assumptions. Managed APIs can be best when the team does not want to operate hardware at all.

items.text: Product framing: choose the hardware path that meets the user promise at the lowest operational burden.
Engineering framing: map the workload to memory, precision, batch shape, data movement, and scaling time.
Finance framing: compare cost per completed useful task, not hourly instance price alone.

blocks.title: Worked beginner artifact: hardware fit card

spans.text: Create one card per workload. Live chat: 7B instruct model, first token under two seconds, context 8k, 20 concurrent users, streaming required, GPU memory and KV cache are the limit. Nightly embeddings: 50,000 chunks, can finish in two hours, batching matters more than first-token latency, retryable on cheaper capacity. Fine-tuning: occasional, checkpointed, can use rented accelerators and stop when metrics plateau.

The card stops magical thinking. It shows that the same team may use CPU workers for orchestration, one GPU endpoint for chat, spot or scheduled GPU jobs for embeddings, and hosted or rented capacity for rare training.

blocks.prompt: What should you ask before choosing GPU, TPU, or CPU?

options.text: Which accelerator has the most impressive benchmark headline?

Which option sounds most advanced?

blocks.explanation: Hardware is useful only in relation to a workload and a product promise.

modules.title: Understand memory, precision, and data movement
modules.sub: See why model weights, activations, KV cache, and input pipelines compete for capacity.
modules.summary: Accelerators are fast when the model fits, data arrives on time, and precision choices preserve acceptable quality.
objectives: Name the main memory consumers in inference and training.
Explain why quantization is a capacity lever.
Identify data loading as a hardware bottleneck.

blocks.title: The accelerator waits for the slowest dependency

spans.text: For LLM inference, memory is consumed by model weights, runtime overhead, and KV cache for active tokens. Longer context and more concurrent requests can run out of memory even when the model weights fit. For training, activations, gradients, optimizer state, and batch size add pressure beyond the raw model file.

Precision changes the tradeoff. Lower precision or quantization can reduce memory and increase feasible throughput, but it must be tested for quality and supported kernels. Data movement matters too: a powerful accelerator can sit idle if preprocessing, disk, or network cannot feed it fast enough.

blocks.title: Case study: the GPU is fast but the service is slow

spans.text: A chat service shows 35 percent GPU utilization and p95 latency above five seconds. The beginner guess is "buy a bigger GPU." The trace shows the real issue: requests queue behind long document-summary jobs, and the model endpoint accepts prompts with huge context windows. Separate batch traffic, cap context for interactive routes, and measure again before changing hardware.
This reinforces module 1: hardware choice follows workload isolation. A powerful chip cannot fix a traffic policy that mixes patient batch work with impatient chat work.

modules.title: Compare CPU, GPU, TPU, and managed capacity
modules.sub: Choose by software ecosystem, scaling behavior, availability, and operational skill.
modules.summary: Each hardware path bundles a software stack and operating model, not just silicon.
objectives: Compare hardware options without one-size-fits-all claims.
Explain when managed APIs beat owning accelerators.
Describe MIG and partitioning as sharing tools, not magic capacity.

blocks.title: Every chip comes with a platform

spans.text: A GPU path usually fits broad PyTorch, CUDA, and serving-engine ecosystems. TPUs fit workloads and frameworks designed for them, often inside a cloud platform. CPUs are easiest to operate but can be too slow for large neural workloads. Managed model APIs shift capacity planning to a provider while reducing low-level control.

NVIDIA MIG is useful when supported hardware can be partitioned into isolated GPU instances for smaller workloads. It improves sharing and isolation, but it does not remove memory limits or make one device equivalent to many full GPUs. TPUs similarly require platform-aware design rather than simple drop-in replacement thinking.

options.name: CPU

cells.text: Orchestration, small ML, preprocessing, light batch jobs
Large neural inference may miss latency or throughput goals

options.whenToUse: Start here when the model is small or latency is loose.

options.name: GPU

cells.text: LLM serving, embeddings, vision, fine-tuning, many PyTorch workloads
Memory, driver/runtime compatibility, cold starts, and idle spend

options.whenToUse: Use when tensor compute and ecosystem support matter.

options.name: TPU or managed accelerator

cells.text: Large training or batch workloads designed for the stack
Framework support, data pipeline design, quota, and portability

options.whenToUse: Use when the platform and workload align.

blocks.ruleOfThumb: Prefer the hardware path your team can keep utilized, observable, and recoverable.
blocks.useWhen: Use owned or reserved accelerators when volume, data locality, and operational skill justify them.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid buying hardware to solve unclear workload shape, missing traces, or a product still changing daily.

modules.title: Estimate capacity with simple checks
modules.sub: Use a small capacity sketch before load tests and procurement.
modules.summary: A practical estimate records model size, memory headroom, concurrency, batch behavior, and cost per useful task.
objectives: Write a simple hardware planning function.
Predict why max concurrency can fail before average load.
Verify AI-generated hardware advice for missing assumptions.

blocks.title: Toy capacity sketch for an LLM endpoint
blocks.code:
model_gb = 14          # rough quantized weight size
gpu_memory_gb = 24
runtime_overhead_gb = 3
kv_cache_per_user_gb = 0.6

available_for_cache = gpu_memory_gb - model_gb - runtime_overhead_gb
max_active_users = int(available_for_cache // kv_cache_per_user_gb)

print({
    "available_for_cache_gb": round(available_for_cache, 1),
    "rough_max_active_users": max_active_users,
})

assert max_active_users > 0, "model fits weights but leaves no room for serving"

spans.text: The numbers are simplified, but the lesson is real: fitting model weights is not the same as serving concurrent users. KV cache, runtime overhead, and context length consume the remaining memory.

predictThenReveal.prompt: If the model weights fit exactly into device memory, is the endpoint ready for chat traffic?
predictThenReveal.answer: No. Serving also needs runtime overhead and KV cache for active tokens, so exact weight fit can still fail under real requests.

spans.text: When an AI assistant recommends "use an A100" or "switch to TPU," demand the missing assumptions. Good advice names workload, framework, model size, precision, context length, batch size, concurrency, latency target, data pipeline, autoscaling behavior, and budget.

items.text: Does the recommendation separate training, batch inference, and interactive serving?
Does it account for memory beyond weights, especially KV cache or optimizer state?
Does it include cold start, quota, driver/runtime, and observability constraints?
Does it compare cost per useful result rather than hourly price only?

blocks.title: Memory trap
blocks.prompt: Why can a model that fits on a GPU still fail under chat load?

options.text: Because GPUs cannot stream text.
Concurrent requests and long contexts need KV cache and runtime memory beyond the weights.
Because CPU orchestration is never required.

blocks.explanation: Serving memory includes active token state and overhead, not just the static model file.

blocks.title: Retrieval prompt for the whole lesson

spans.text: Answer this without notes: "How do I decide whether an AI workload needs CPU, GPU, TPU, or a managed API?" A good answer starts with workload type, latency target, memory, batch behavior, data movement, software ecosystem, utilization, and cost per useful result.
Spaced recall: return to the first module. The question was never "Which chip is best?" It was "Which workload promise must be met, and what hardware path can the team operate honestly?"

blocks.ruleOfThumb: Buy or rent capacity only after workload evidence exists.
blocks.useWhen: Use accelerators when traces or load tests show tensor compute and memory are the binding constraints.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid procurement based on benchmark headlines, model popularity, or a single happy-path demo.

blocks.title: Capstone: hardware fit card for one feature

spans.text: Choose one feature, such as live lesson chat or nightly embedding refresh. Fill out: model, input size, output size, precision, latency target, concurrency, batch window, memory estimate, data source, retry plan, observability fields, and cost per useful result. Recommend CPU, GPU, TPU, or managed API and list the first load test you would run.
Next rung: connect this to cost and latency optimization, where the same hardware decision becomes part of a route, cache, and budget policy.

gpu.label: GPU
gpu.laymanDefinition: A processor built to run many math operations in parallel.
gpu.technicalNote: For learners, a GPU is useful when tensor math is the bottleneck and the model plus working memory fit the device.

serving.label: Serving
serving.laymanDefinition: Keeping a model ready so users can call it.
serving.technicalNote: Hardware serving decisions balance warm weights, KV cache, batch size, streaming latency, and how slowly accelerators scale up.

gateway.label: Gateway
gateway.laymanDefinition: The traffic controller in front of model hardware.
gateway.technicalNote: A gateway can route light work to CPU or small GPUs, reserve larger accelerators for hard requests, and enforce budgets.

latency.label: Latency
latency.laymanDefinition: How long a user waits for a result.
latency.technicalNote: Hardware can reduce compute time but still lose to queueing, cold starts, network transfer, or oversized context.

throughput.label: Throughput
throughput.laymanDefinition: How many predictions, tokens, images, or training steps finish over time.
throughput.technicalNote: Throughput improves when the workload batches well and keeps the accelerator fed with data.

versioning.label: Versioning
versioning.laymanDefinition: Recording the hardware and runtime shape used for a result.
versioning.technicalNote: For reproducibility, capture accelerator type, precision, quantization, driver/runtime, batch limits, and model version.

finalCheck.title: Knowledge check
finalCheck.intro: A quick check across the whole lesson — pick or type your answers.

questions.prompt: You're launching a chatbot that must respond to each user within 2 seconds. Which workload type best describes this, and why does it matter for hardware selection?

options.text: Batch inference — you can queue requests and process them together overnight, so raw throughput is the priority.
Interactive serving — low latency per request is the priority, so memory bandwidth and fast token generation matter more than peak throughput.
Training — you need the most FLOPS possible to update model weights in real time.
Batch inference — grouping user requests into large batches minimizes cost and meets the 2-second target easily.

questions.explanation: Interactive serving is defined by strict per-request latency requirements; memory bandwidth (how fast the chip feeds data to compute) often limits token generation speed more than raw FLOPS.

questions.prompt: A 70-billion-parameter model stored in 16-bit precision needs roughly 140 GB of GPU memory just for weights. A team wants to serve it on a single GPU with 80 GB of VRAM. Which technique is the most direct lever to make the weights fit?

options.text: Use a faster interconnect between GPUs.
Switch to a larger batch size to amortize memory cost.
Quantize the model to 8-bit or 4-bit precision to shrink weight size.
Enable Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitioning on the single GPU.

questions.explanation: Quantization reduces the number of bits used to store each weight, directly shrinking total memory footprint — halving precision roughly halves the memory required for weights.

questions.prompt: A startup runs occasional, unpredictable spikes of AI inference — sometimes zero traffic, sometimes a burst of thousands of requests. Which hardware approach is most likely to give the best cost per useful result?

options.text: Buy and co-locate dedicated H100 GPUs to guarantee capacity at all times.
Use a managed API (e.g., a cloud model endpoint) so you pay per request and avoid idle hardware costs.
Deploy a TPU pod reserved for 3 years to lock in the lowest per-hour rate.
Use MIG partitioning on a single on-premise GPU to serve all traffic.

questions.explanation: Managed APIs charge per token or per request, so idle time costs nothing — this beats owning accelerators when traffic is unpredictable and utilization would otherwise be low.

questions.prompt: Explain in plain language why a system can run out of capacity during a sudden traffic spike even when its *average* load looks fine on a dashboard.
questions.acceptableAnswer: Average load hides peaks. If requests arrive in bursts, the queue of concurrent requests can exceed the maximum the hardware can hold in memory or process simultaneously — even if the hourly or daily average looks low. Max concurrency (the worst-case simultaneous demand) is what causes failures, not the average.
questions.explanation: Averages smooth over spikes; hardware fails at peak concurrency, not average load, so planning only to average demand leaves a system vulnerable to burst failures.

questions.prompt: An AI assistant recommends a specific GPU configuration for your workload but doesn't mention the model's sequence length, batch size, or whether you need training or inference. What is the most important reason to flag this advice as incomplete?

options.text: GPU recommendations are always wrong unless they come from the chip manufacturer.
Hardware fit depends on workload assumptions; missing those means the recommendation could be wildly over- or under-provisioned for your actual needs.
The advice is fine — GPU choice only depends on budget, not workload details.
Sequence length and batch size only matter for TPUs, not GPUs.

questions.explanation: Hardware sizing is always conditional on workload specifics (model size, precision, sequence length, concurrency targets); a recommendation without those assumptions cannot be verified or trusted.
